Delay-Doppler cell¶

Summary¶

A GNSS-R receiver does not see the surface as one big patch. It compares the reflected signal against a copy of the GNSS code (this sorts the surface by delay) and runs a Fourier transform over the integration time (this sorts it by Doppler, i.e. by range-rate). The result is a Delay-Doppler Map (DDM), and one pixel is the surface patch having both the selected delay and Doppler.

This module estimates that area locally from first derivatives. Away from singular geometries it can be much smaller than the antenna footprint. At the exact specular point the first-order mapping is singular, so this implementation deliberately falls back to the footprint area; it does not currently produce a small specular DDM cell from second-order delay curvature.

Detailed Module Description¶

Two fields on the surface¶

Every point on the sea has a delay and a Doppler, set by two fields. The first is the total path length the signal travels, transmitter to surface to receiver,

(26)¶\[L(\mathbf{r}) = R_t(\mathbf{r}) + R_r(\mathbf{r}),\]

which fixes the delay (delay is just \(L/c\)). The second is the Doppler shift, set by the satellite velocities relative to the rotating surface,

(27)¶\[f_D(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\,\left[ \hat{n}_{tx2s}\cdot(\mathbf{v}_{tx}-\mathbf{v}_{s}) - \hat{n}_{s2rx}\cdot(\mathbf{v}_{rx}-\mathbf{v}_{s})\right],\]

with carrier wavelength \(\lambda\) and \(\mathbf{v}_s=\boldsymbol{\omega}_E\times\mathbf{r}\).

How fast the fields change across the surface¶

To turn “one chip of delay” and “one Doppler bin” into an area, we need how quickly each field changes as you move across the surface – its gradient in the local tangent plane. For the path length this is the scattering vector,

(28)¶\[\nabla L = \hat{n}_{tx2s} - \hat{n}_{s2rx},\]

and for the Doppler it comes from the parts of the satellite velocities that point across the line of sight (not along it),

(29)¶\[\nabla f_D = \frac{1}{\lambda}\left( \frac{\mathbf{v}_{tx,rel,\perp}}{R_t} + \frac{\mathbf{v}_{rx,rel,\perp}}{R_r} + \boldsymbol{\omega}_E\times(\hat{n}_{tx2s}-\hat{n}_{s2rx})\right).\]

The final term is the spatial derivative of the rigid-rotation velocity. Both gradients are projected onto the tangent plane (the part along the surface normal is dropped).

The cell area¶

One code chip is a step in path length of \(\delta L = c / R_\mathrm{chip}\) (for GPS C/A, \(R_\mathrm{chip} = 1.023\) Mcps, so \(\delta L \approx 293\) m), and one Doppler bin is \(\delta f_D = 1 / T_\mathrm{coh}\). Because both gradients lie in the same flat tangent plane, the size of the (delay, Doppler) -> (surface) mapping is just the size of their cross product,

(30)¶\[|\det J| = |\nabla L \times \nabla f_D| \quad [\mathrm{Hz/m}],\]

and the area of the surface patch that falls into one chip-by-one-bin box is

(31)¶\[A_\mathrm{cell} = \frac{\delta L \; \delta f_D}{|\det J|} \quad [\mathrm{m}^2].\]

A longer integration time \(T_\mathrm{coh}\) makes the Doppler bins narrower and the cell smaller.

The near-specular cap¶

At the specular reflection point the path length is at its minimum, so \(\nabla L \to 0\), the Jacobian goes to zero, and the formula blows up – the iso-delay rings are genuinely far apart at the glint. The same can happen when \(\nabla f_D \to 0\). In those cases the cell is capped at the antenna footprint area, the largest patch the receiver could integrate. In backscatter mode the reflection point sits well away from the delay minimum, so the cell is well-defined; the cap mainly matters in the forward/specular direction.

API reference¶

functions.delay_doppler.delay_doppler_cell_area(geometry, tx_velocities_eci, rx_velocities_eci, wavelength_m, chip_length_m, coherent_integration_time_s, footprint_area_m2=None, surface_positions_eci=None)[source]¶

Delay-Doppler resolution-cell area per sample from the (delay, Doppler) -> surface Jacobian.

Parameters:

  • geometry (BistaticGeometry) – Per-sample directions and ranges (n samples).

  • tx_velocities_eci (numpy.ndarray) – Transmitter ECI velocities [m/s], shape (3, n).

  • rx_velocities_eci (numpy.ndarray) – Receiver ECI velocities [m/s], shape (3, n).

  • wavelength_m (float) – Carrier wavelength [m].

  • chip_length_m (float) – One code-chip path length delta_L = c / R_chip [m].

  • coherent_integration_time_s (float) – Coherent integration time T_coh [s]; the Doppler bin is 1 / T_coh.

  • footprint_area_m2 (numpy.ndarray or float or None) – Upper-bound cap (antenna footprint area) [m^2]; None means no cap.

  • surface_positions_eci (numpy.ndarray or None) – Surface positions [m], shape (n, 3). When supplied, rigid Earth rotation is included in the Doppler field and its spatial gradient. None retains a stationary-in-ECI surface.

Returns:

Per-sample (n,) arrays: cell_area_m2 (footprint-capped cell area), uncapped_cell_area_m2, delay_width_m (delta_L / |grad L|), doppler_width_m (delta_fD / |grad f_D|), delay_gradient (|grad L|), doppler_gradient_hz_m (|grad f_D|), abs_jacobian_det_hz_m (|grad L x grad f_D|), and footprint_capped (True where the cap or a near-specular degeneracy set the area to the footprint).

Return type:

dict

Module Assumptions and Limitations¶

  • First-order (linear) cell. The area uses the first derivatives of the delay and Doppler fields. This is accurate away from the specular point but breaks down at the glint, where it is capped at the footprint. The exact near-specular cell (from the curvature of the path length) is a future refinement.

  • No target-to-cell membership test. The moving-target pipeline first checks antenna-footprint overlap. It does not yet compute the ship’s own delay and Doppler and prove that the target and the ocean reference point occupy the same DDM bin. Therefore DDM-cell clutter results are a sensitivity approximation, not a complete detector simulation.

  • Code chip sets the delay size. For spread signals (BOC, CBOC, AltBOC) the base code-chip rate is used, which is the conservative (coarser delay, larger cell) choice. Chip rates live per (constellation, band) in Constants.GNSS_CHIP_RATE_HZ.

  • No geometry change during integration. The cell is computed at one instant; smearing from the satellites moving during \(T_\mathrm{coh}\) is not modelled.

  • Cap needs a footprint. Without a footprint area the near-specular cell is left as NaN rather than bounded.

Validation and Tests¶

Test group

What it checks

TestJacobianAgainstFiniteDifferences

The analytic Jacobian and delay gradient match direct finite differences, including a rotating surface case.

TestChipLength

The GPS C/A chip is 293.05 m (c / 1.023 MHz).

TestScaling

The area grows with the chip length and shrinks with the integration time, exactly as the formula says.

TestFootprintCap / TestDegenerateAndInvalid

A small footprint caps the cell; a large one does not; a near-specular case collapses to the footprint; invalid geometry returns NaN.

TestOrderOfMagnitude

A representative non-specular geometry lands in a broad plausibility range. This is not external instrument validation.

TestChipRateTable / TestSettingsValidation

The chip-rate lookups work and every EIRP band has a chip rate; the cell setting requires a coherent time and is mutually exclusive with patch integration.

User Guide¶

The cell is turned on in the moving-target link budget through [LINK BUDGET]:

Key

Meaning

Unit

delay_doppler_cell_enabled

Use one DDM cell as the ocean-clutter area instead of the footprint.

boolean

coherent_integration_time_s

Coherent integration time T_coh; sets the Doppler bin 1 / T_coh. Required when the cell is on.

s

When enabled, compute_reflection_link_budget() calls this module and uses the cell area as the distributed-clutter area. The chip length comes from the band’s chip rate (c / chip_rate). Check footprint_capped before interpreting a result: exact specular samples normally use the footprint cap in the present first-order implementation.

References¶

  • Zavorotny, V. & Voronovich, A., “Scattering of GPS signals from the ocean with wind remote sensing application”, IEEE TGRS 38(2), 2000.

  • Clarizia, M. P. et al., “Analysis of GNSS-R delay-Doppler maps from the UK-DMC satellite over the ocean”, Geophysical Research Letters 36, 2009.
